summary:
LUNA SIGHT is a next-generation mission control and analysis station—inspired by NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) architecture—designed to evaluate candidate landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole (notably "Connecting Ridge/Site01" and "Shackleton Rim/Site04"). It utilizes real-time ephemeris data, high-resolution topographic horizon models, and AI-driven visual analysis.

Developed in alignment with the vision of the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the project models critical parameters for Artemis mission landing planning—such as solar illumination duration, direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility, topographic horizon obstructions, and Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) within crater floors—all within a single, coordinated interface.
details:
# LUNA SIGHT

## Lunar south pole landing-site analysis for NASA Space Apps

### Project overview

LUNA SIGHT is an interactive mission-planning workstation that helps teams compare where and when to land near the Moon’s south pole. It brings together three questions that are easy to examine separately and consequential to answer together. When is the Sun visible from a candidate site? When does that same site have a direct line of sight to Earth? How long do those conditions overlap?

The project combines NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides, lunar elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, and an interactive 3D Moon Trek view. It turns those inputs into visibility timelines, outage estimates, and candidate operating windows. Users can inspect the terrain behind a result, compare sites under the same assumptions, and review the data used to make the comparison.

### Why this problem matters

The Sun stays close to the horizon near the lunar south pole. A ridge may have a clear view of the Sun while a nearby crater floor remains in shadow. Earth follows a different path across the local sky, and lunar libration changes its apparent position over time. A crater wall can therefore block Earth for long periods even when the site remains illuminated.

Consider a solar-powered surface mission that needs direct communications with Earth. A site with continuous modeled sunlight may appear attractive on an illumination map, yet the mission could arrive during a prolonged communications outage. Conversely, a site with a limited window may support the planned operation if the window opens at the right time and lasts long enough. LUNA SIGHT evaluates the site and the timing together, using the terrain in the direction of each body at each point in the analysis.

### How LUNA SIGHT works

**1. Compute the local sky geometry.** The project uses NASA JPL Horizons and the DE441 ephemeris to obtain the Sun’s and Earth’s azimuth and elevation from a specified point on the lunar surface. Azimuth tells the system which direction to look. Elevation gives the body’s angle above or below the local horizontal plane. The reference case uses a five-minute sampling interval, yielding 2,017 timestamps per site over 168 hours, including both endpoints. Calculating from the lunar surface accounts for observer parallax. The project reports an Earth elevation difference of about 0.24° when the observer’s surface position is omitted, large enough to affect a near-horizon visibility decision.

**2. Build a terrain horizon for each site.** The topography module uses digital elevation models derived from Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data. For the reference comparison, it uses a 5 m/pixel local model and a 4 km search radius. The system traces rays around the full 360° horizon and records the highest terrain obstruction angle in each direction. This produces a profile that can represent a high crater wall on one side and a depression on the other. Data-quality flags preserve gaps so downstream analysis can account for incomplete terrain coverage.

**3. Evaluate Sun and Earth visibility independently.** At each timestamp, the engine subtracts the terrain horizon angle at the body’s azimuth from the body’s elevation angle. A clearance above +0.10° is classified as visible. A clearance below −0.10° is classified as blocked. Values within the band, including its boundaries, are uncertain. Linear interpolation between samples estimates transition times. A transition displayed to the second reflects the interpolation output, while the underlying terrain and geometry still determine its accuracy.

**4. Assemble windows and compare mission constraints.** The engine calculates sunlight, direct-to-Earth visibility, and the overlap between them. A joint window requires both bodies to be classified as visible. The workstation presents durations, the longest continuous window, and communications outages. Users can compare scenarios against adjustable criteria, including minimum sunlight and maximum tolerable blackout. A favorable interval supports an operation scheduled within that interval. A full-week assessment also accounts for outages before and after it.

### What the reference case shows

The project compares Connecting Ridge (Site01) and Shackleton Rim (Site04) from 14 November 2026 at 00:00 UTC to 21 November 2026 at 00:00 UTC. Both candidate points have 168 hours of modeled Sun visibility. Their direct-to-Earth results differ sharply.

**Connecting Ridge** has **53.68 continuous hours** of joint Sun and Earth visibility, approximately **31.96%** of the period. The window begins at approximately **18:18:55 UTC on 18 November** and extends to the end of the modeled interval. The terrain horizon in the direction of Earth ranges from approximately +0.82° to +1.06°. As Earth rises above that horizon, the modeled clearance reaches about +2.96°. The window gives planners a specific interval to examine for operations that require both conditions.

**Shackleton Rim** has **zero hours** of direct Earth visibility and **zero hours** of joint visibility during the same period. In the directions Earth occupies, terrain rises approximately +6.43° to +9.24° above the local horizontal plane. Earth reaches about +4.14° at its highest point during the case, leaving its line of sight blocked. Meanwhile, the Sun remains visible in a different direction, where the terrain horizon is lower. The result shows why an average horizon angle or an illumination percentage alone can conceal a communications constraint. [Reference run and results](https://github.com/kingos352/luna-sight/blob/main/docs/REAL_RUN.md)

The team also tested how modeling assumptions change the result. At Connecting Ridge, the 2 km and 4 km profiles at 5 m/pixel gave the same 53.68-hour result. A 20 km comparison using a coarser 240 m/pixel regional model yielded 87.88 hours. The coarser grid smooths local terrain that can obstruct the view, so the project uses the high-resolution local result for its headline comparison. Varying the uncertainty band from ±0.05° to ±0.20° changed the modeled joint visibility at Connecting Ridge from 32.47% to 30.93%. [Sensitivity analysis](https://github.com/kingos352/luna-sight/blob/main/docs/REAL_RUN.md#5-duyarlılık)

### What users can do with the workstation

The interface is inspired by NASA’s General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). Users can explore candidate sites on a 3D lunar globe, inspect crater rims and terrain, and scrub through the scenario timeline. An inspection panel shows Sun and Earth geometry alongside the calculated terrain clearance. The side-by-side comparison helps users trace a blackout to a specific portion of the local horizon and see when it begins or ends. A downloadable flight card captures the selected scenario and its mission constraints for review.

The project also includes an optional image-analysis assistant that describes visible surface features in terrain imagery. Its observations help users explore the scene. The ephemeris, terrain model, and visibility engine provide the quantitative values used in the mission comparison. [Project repository](https://github.com/kingos352/luna-sight) · [Surface analysis documentation](https://github.com/kingos352/luna-sight/blob/main/docs/AI_SURFACE_ANALYSIS.md)

### Verification and scope

The repository publishes the analysis code, data contracts, reference outputs, and instructions for reproducing the case study. SHA-256 hashes help identify the source responses used for the calculation. The repository documents a run of 265 automated tests covering ephemerides, terrain profiles, visibility logic, site handling, 3D components, and the image-analysis integration. [Verification and data provenance](https://github.com/kingos352/luna-sight#7-test-ve-doğrulama-verification-suite)

The case evaluates specific observer points and a single seven-day interval. The 5 m/pixel figure describes the elevation grid spacing. Parts of that grid are interpolated, and terrain uncertainty can shift predicted horizon crossings. Direct Earth visibility describes geometric clearance. An operational communications assessment would also consider antenna pointing, radio link margin, ground-station availability, and any relay coverage. Solar power availability likewise depends on factors such as panel orientation, terrain shadowing, and the spacecraft’s energy budget. These distinctions make the workstation suitable for early site screening, scenario comparison, and education.

### Intended impact

LUNA SIGHT gives Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services planners a way to compare candidate sites and dates using the same set of inputs. If a schedule shifts, a team can examine how the new dates change the overlap between sunlight and direct Earth visibility. An extended blackout can prompt a closer look at a different surface location, a shorter operating interval, or relay coverage. For educators, the 3D view makes it possible to demonstrate how the same crater rim can leave the Sun visible while hiding Earth.

The reference case captures the project’s purpose. Two candidate sites offer the same week of sunlight, yet only one provides a period of direct Earth visibility. LUNA SIGHT shows when that difference matters, which terrain creates it, and which assumptions a planner should carry into the next analysis.
